statement: Let $\Lambda(n) = \log p$ if $n = p^k$ for a prime $p$ and $k \ge 1$, and $\Lambda(n) = 0$ otherwise. For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series) $\sum \Lambda(n) n^{-s}$ converges absolutely and equals $-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)$, where $\zeta$ is the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function).

hypotheses.text: The number $s$ lies in the [half-plane](c:half-plane) $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$.
The function $\zeta(s) = \sum n^{-s}$ is the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function) on this half-plane.

conclusion: The series $\sum \Lambda(n) n^{-s}$ converges absolutely, $\zeta(s) \ne 0$, and the series equals the negative [logarithmic derivative](c:logarithmic-derivative) $-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)$; for real $s > 1$ it also equals $\sum_p (\log p)/(p^s - 1)$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the identity $L(\Lambda, s) = -\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ only. It does not state the divisor identity, the absolute convergence or the sum over primes.

proofs.name: Dirichlet product with zeta
proofs.slogan: Multiply the von Mangoldt series by zeta to get the series of the logarithm, then divide.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem under the two hypotheses. The prime form is for real $s > 1$ only.

roles.why: The half-plane gives absolute convergence of every series, and uniform convergence on closed half-planes.
The zeta series is the Dirichlet series that the proof multiplies, differentiates and inverts.

steps.slogan: Sum the values of $\Lambda$ over the divisors of $n$ to get $\log n$.
steps.detail: Write $n = \prod p_i^{a_i}$. The divisors $d$ with $\Lambda(d) \ne 0$ are the prime powers $p_i^k$ with $1 \le k \le a_i$. Each has $\Lambda(d) = \log p_i$, so the sum is $\sum a_i \log p_i = \log n$.

steps.slogan: Bound $\Lambda(n) n^{-\sigma}$ by a convergent power of $n$ to get [absolute convergence](c:absolute-convergence).
steps.detail: Let $\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s > 1$ and $\varepsilon = (\sigma - 1)/2$. Then $0 \le \Lambda(n) \le \log n \le n^{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon$, so $\Lambda(n) n^{-\sigma} \le \frac{2}{\sigma - 1} n^{-(1+\sigma)/2}$. This series converges because $(1+\sigma)/2 > 1$.

steps.slogan: Turn the divisor identity into a product of [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series).
steps.detail: The identity says $\Lambda * 1 = \log$ for [arithmetic functions](c:arithmetic-function). All three series converge absolutely for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. So $L(\Lambda, s)\,\zeta(s) = \sum (\log n) n^{-s}$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the zeta series term by term to get $\zeta'(s) = -\sum (\log n) n^{-s}$.
steps.detail: The term $n^{-s}$ has derivative $-(\log n) n^{-s}$. On $\operatorname{Re} s \ge \sigma_0 > 1$ the M-test with $(\log n) n^{-\sigma_0}$ gives [uniform convergence](c:uniform-convergence). A uniform limit of holomorphic functions has the termwise derivative.

steps.slogan: Show that $\zeta(s)$ is not zero for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$.
steps.detail: The series $\sum \mu(n) n^{-s}$ converges absolutely for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. By the product rule it is the inverse series of $\zeta(s)$. So $\zeta(s) \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Divide the product identity by $\zeta(s)$ to get $-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $L(\Lambda, s)\,\zeta(s) = -\zeta'(s)$. Step 5 allows the division by $\zeta(s)$. So $L(\Lambda, s) = -\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)$, the negative [logarithmic derivative](c:logarithmic-derivative) of $\zeta$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the series for real $s > 1$ as a sum over primes.
steps.detail: Only prime powers contribute, so the series is $\sum_p \sum_{k \ge 1} (\log p) p^{-ks}$. All terms are positive, so the order of summation is free. The inner geometric series has the value $(\log p)/(p^s - 1)$.

concepts.c:dirichlet-series: The proof multiplies and inverts Dirichlet series.
concepts.c:riemann-zeta-function: Zeta is the series that carries the identity.
concepts.c:half-plane: All convergence claims hold on the half-plane $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$.
concepts.c:logarithmic-derivative: The result says that the von Mangoldt series is minus this quotient.
concepts.c:absolute-convergence: Absolute convergence allows the product and the rearrangement of series.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence allows the termwise derivative of the zeta series.
concepts.c:arithmetic-function: The divisor identity is an identity of arithmetic functions.

statement: Let $A$ be an [integrally closed domain](c:integrally-closed-domain) with fraction field $K$, $L/K$ a finite [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) with group $G$, and $B$ the [integral closure](c:integral-closure) of $A$ in $L$. Prime ideals $P, Q$ of $B$ over a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ satisfy $Q = \sigma(P)$ for some $\sigma \in G$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $A$ is an [integrally closed domain](c:integrally-closed-domain) with fraction field $K$.
The extension $L/K$ is a finite [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) with group $G$.
The ring $B$ is the [integral closure](c:integral-closure) of $A$ in $L$.
The ideal $\mathfrak p$ is a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) of $A$.
The ideals $P$ and $Q$ are [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) of $B$ with $P \cap A = Q \cap A = \mathfrak p$.

conclusion: There is $\sigma \in G$ with $Q = \sigma(P)$, and $P$ and $Q$ have the same [ramification index](c:ramification-index) over $\mathfrak p$ and the same residue degree.

formal.difference: The declaration states the transitivity $\sigma P = Q$ only. Equal ramification index and equal residue degree are separate facts.

proofs.name: Product over the Galois group
proofs.slogan: Assume Q is not a conjugate of P, and multiply the conjugates of a separating element to reach a contradiction.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The equality of the indices is read from the automorphism $\sigma$ with $\sigma(P) = Q$.

roles.why: The group $G$ is finite and its fixed field is $K$, so the product over $G$ lies in $K$.
The ring $B$ is stable under $G$, so $G$ acts on its ideals.
The ring $A/\mathfrak p$ is a field, so every prime over $\mathfrak p$ is maximal.
The primes $P$ and $Q$ both contain $\mathfrak p$, which makes the product land in $P$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G$ acts on $B$ and sends primes over $\mathfrak p$ to primes over $\mathfrak p$.
steps.detail: For $\sigma \in G$ and $b \in B$, the element $\sigma(b)$ satisfies the same monic equation over $A$ as $b$. So $\sigma(b) \in B$. Hence $\sigma$ is a ring automorphism of $B$ that fixes $A$, and $\sigma(P)$ is a prime ideal over $\mathfrak p$.

steps.slogan: Show that every prime ideal of $B$ over $\mathfrak p$ is maximal.
steps.detail: The ring $B/P$ is a domain that is integral over the field $A/\mathfrak p$. A domain that is integral over a field is a field. So $P$ is maximal, and so are $Q$ and every $\sigma(P)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the elements of $B$ fixed by $G$ are exactly the elements of $A$.
steps.detail: We have $B^G = B \cap L^G = B \cap K$. An element of $K$ that is integral over $A$ lies in $A$, because $A$ is [integrally closed](c:integrally-closed-domain). So $B^G = A$.

steps.slogan: Assume that $Q \ne \sigma(P)$ for all $\sigma$ and pick $x \in Q$ outside every $\sigma(P)$.
steps.detail: The ideals $\sigma(P)$ are finitely many and maximal. If $Q \subseteq \sigma(P)$, then $Q = \sigma(P)$ by maximality. So $Q$ lies in none of them, and prime avoidance gives $x \in Q$ with $x \notin \sigma(P)$ for all $\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the conjugates of $x$ to get an element of $\mathfrak p$ and a contradiction.
steps.detail: Put $y = \prod_{\sigma \in G} \sigma(x)$. It lies in $B^G = A$, and in $Q$ because the factor for $\sigma = 1$ is $x$. So $y \in Q \cap A = \mathfrak p \subseteq P$. As $P$ is prime, some $\sigma(x) \in P$, so $x \in \sigma^{-1}(P)$. This contradicts the choice of $x$.

steps.slogan: Move $P$ to $Q$ by $\sigma$ and compare ramification indices and residue degrees.
steps.detail: Let $\sigma(P) = Q$. Then $\sigma(\mathfrak p B) = \mathfrak p B$, so $\mathfrak p B \subseteq P^e$ if and only if $\mathfrak p B \subseteq Q^e$. Hence the indices are equal. Also $b + P \mapsto \sigma(b) + Q$ is an $A/\mathfrak p$-linear ring isomorphism $B/P \to B/Q$, so the residue degrees are equal.

concepts.c:galois-extension: The fixed field of $G$ is $K$, so the norm lies in $K$.
concepts.c:integral-closure: The ring $B$ is the stable ring on which $G$ acts.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: Maximality makes every prime over $\mathfrak p$ maximal.
concepts.c:prime-ideal: Primality of $P$ turns a product in $P$ into a factor in $P$.
concepts.c:ramification-index: The automorphism $\sigma$ carries the index of $P$ to the index of $Q$.

statement: Let $F$ be a [finite field](c:finite-field) with $q$ elements and $L$ an extension of $F$ of degree $n$. Then $\varphi(x) = x^q$ has order $n$ and $L/F$ is [Galois](c:galois-extension) with cyclic group $\langle \varphi \rangle$. For each divisor $d$ of $n$, the set $E_d = \{x \in L : x^{q^d} = x\}$ is the unique [intermediate field](c:intermediate-field) of degree $d$ over $F$.

hypotheses.text: The field $F$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field) with $q$ elements.
The field $L$ is a [field extension](c:field-extension) of $F$ of finite degree $n$.

conclusion: The group $\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)$ is cyclic of order $n$ and generated by $\varphi$; every intermediate field is some $E_d$ with $d \mid n$; $E_d \subseteq E_e$ if and only if $d \mid e$; $\#\{x \in L : x^{q^d} = x\} = q^{\gcd(d, n)}$; and a finite extension $E$ of $F$ embeds in $L$ if and only if $[E : F]$ divides $n$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the Frobenius algebra map has order equal to the degree of the extension. The Galois group, the subfields, the root count and the embedding criterion are separate facts.

proofs.name: Frobenius and Artin
proofs.slogan: Show that Frobenius has order n, then use Artin and the cyclic subgroups to read off the subfields.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The count and the embedding criterion use that the group is generated by $\varphi$ with $\varphi^n = \mathrm{id}$.

roles.why: The field $F$ gives $a^q = a$ on $F$, and $|L| = q^n$ gives $x^{q^n} = x$ on $L$.
The finite degree $n$ fixes the size of $L$ and the order of the group.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi$ is an $F$-automorphism of $L$.
steps.detail: The map $x \mapsto x^q$ is additive and multiplicative, because $q$ is a power of the characteristic. It is injective on a field, so it is bijective on the finite set $L$. For $a \in F^\times$, Lagrange gives $a^{q-1} = 1$, so $\varphi$ fixes $F$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi$ has order exactly $n$.
steps.detail: The group $L^\times$ has $q^n - 1$ elements, so $x^{q^n} = x$ for all $x \in L$ and $\varphi^n = \mathrm{id}$. For $1 \le k < n$, the polynomial $X^{q^k} - X$ has at most $q^k < q^n$ roots in $L$, so $\varphi^k \ne \mathrm{id}$.

steps.slogan: Apply Artin's theorem to $H = \langle \varphi \rangle$ to show that $L/F$ is [Galois](c:galois-extension) with group $H$.
steps.detail: The fixed field $L^H$ contains $F$. Artin's theorem gives $[L : L^H] = |H| = n = [L : F]$, so $L^H = F$. Artin also shows that $L/L^H$ is Galois with group $H$.

steps.slogan: List the subgroups of the [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) $H$ and match them with the intermediate fields.
steps.detail: The subgroups of $H$ are the groups $\langle \varphi^d \rangle$ for $d \mid n$. By the Galois correspondence their fixed fields are the fields $E_d$ of degree $d$, and these are all the intermediate fields. Also $E_d \subseteq E_e$ if and only if $\langle \varphi^e \rangle \subseteq \langle \varphi^d \rangle$, that is $d \mid e$.

steps.slogan: Read off the solution count and the embedding criterion from the subfields.
steps.detail: Let $g = \gcd(d, n)$. Since $\varphi^n = \mathrm{id}$, we have $\langle \varphi^d \rangle = \langle \varphi^g \rangle$, so $x^{q^d} = x$ if and only if $x \in E_g$, which gives $q^g$ solutions. An $F$-map $E \to L$ has an intermediate field as image, so $[E : F] \mid n$. Conversely, $E$ and $E_d$ are splitting fields of $X^{q^d} - X$, so they are isomorphic.

concepts.c:finite-field: The size $q$ of the field gives the Frobenius map and the root bound.
concepts.c:galois-extension: Artin's theorem shows that the extension is Galois.
concepts.c:intermediate-field: The subfields $E_d$ are the intermediate fields that the proof lists.
concepts.c:field-extension: The degree $n$ of the extension sets the order of Frobenius.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: A cyclic group has exactly one subgroup for each divisor of its order.

statement: Let $L/K$ be a finite [field extension](c:field-extension) of degree $n$, and let $K$ contain a primitive $n$-th [root of unity](c:root-of-unity). Then these are equivalent: (1) $L/K$ is Galois with cyclic group; (2) $L$ is a splitting field of an irreducible polynomial $X^n - a$ over $K$; (3) $L = K(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha$ with $\alpha^n \in K$.

hypotheses.text: The extension $L/K$ is a finite [field extension](c:field-extension) of degree $n$.
The field $K$ contains an element $\zeta$ of multiplicative order exactly $n$, a primitive $n$-th [root of unity](c:root-of-unity).

conclusion: The three conditions are equivalent, and then $\sigma \mapsto \sigma(\alpha)/\alpha$ is a group isomorphism from $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ onto the group $\mu_n$ of $n$-th roots of unity in $K$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the equivalence of the three conditions. It does not state the isomorphism $\sigma \mapsto \sigma(\alpha)/\alpha$ onto $\mu_n$.

proofs.name: Eigenvector of the generator
proofs.slogan: Build an eigenvector of a generator of the group, then show that its n-th power lies in K.
proofs.scope: The three implications (1) to (3), (3) to (2) and (2) to (1), then the character. The case $n = 1$ is trivial.

roles.why: The degree $n$ gives $|G| = n$, the degree of the minimal polynomial and the size of the group of the character.
The element $\zeta$ gives the eigenvalue, the $n$ distinct conjugates and the separability of $X^n - a$.

steps.slogan: Build a nonzero eigenvector $\alpha$ of the generator $\sigma$ with eigenvalue $\zeta$.
steps.detail: Let $\sigma$ generate the cyclic group $G$ of order $n$. The maps $\sigma^i$ are linearly independent over $L$. So $\alpha = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \zeta^{-i} \sigma^i(\theta)$ is nonzero for some $\theta \in L$, and $\sigma(\alpha) = \zeta \alpha$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\alpha$ has $n$ distinct conjugates, so $K(\alpha) = L$.
steps.detail: We have $\sigma^i(\alpha) = \zeta^i \alpha$, and these $n$ values are distinct because $\zeta$ has order $n$. So $[K(\alpha) : K] \ge n$. As $K(\alpha) \subseteq L$ and $[L : K] = n$, we get $K(\alpha) = L$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\alpha^n$ is fixed by $G$, so $\alpha^n \in K$.
steps.detail: We have $\sigma(\alpha^n) = \zeta^n \alpha^n = \alpha^n$. So $\alpha^n$ is fixed by $G$. The fixed field of $G$ is $K$, so $\alpha^n \in K$. This proves (3).

steps.slogan: Derive (2) from (3): the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ is $X^n - a$.
steps.detail: Let $\alpha^n = a \in K$ and $L = K(\alpha)$. The minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ has degree $n$ and divides $X^n - a$, so it equals $X^n - a$, which is [irreducible](c:irreducible-polynomial). Its roots $\zeta^i \alpha$ lie in $L$, so $L$ is a splitting field.

steps.slogan: Derive from (2) that $L/K$ is [Galois](c:galois-extension).
steps.detail: The order of $\zeta$ shows that the characteristic of $K$ does not divide $n$. For $n > 1$, $a \ne 0$, because $X^n$ is reducible. So $X^n - a$ has the $n$ distinct roots $\zeta^i \alpha$. A splitting field of a separable polynomial is Galois.

steps.slogan: Define $\chi(\sigma) = \sigma(\alpha)/\alpha$ and show that $\chi$ is a homomorphism into $\mu_n$.
steps.detail: The element $\sigma(\alpha)$ is a root of $X^n - a$, so $\chi(\sigma) \in \mu_n$. For $\sigma, \tau \in G$, $\chi(\tau)$ lies in $K$ and $\sigma$ fixes it. So $\chi(\sigma\tau) = \sigma(\chi(\tau)\alpha)/\alpha = \chi(\sigma)\chi(\tau)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\chi$ is injective, so $G$ is [cyclic](c:cyclic-group) and $\chi$ is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: If $\chi(\sigma) = 1$, then $\sigma(\alpha) = \alpha$, so $\sigma = \mathrm{id}$ because $L = K(\alpha)$. The group $\mu_n$ is cyclic, so its subgroup $\chi(G)$ and the group $G$ are cyclic. Since $|G| = n = |\mu_n|$, the map $\chi$ is an isomorphism.

concepts.c:field-extension: The degree $n$ of the extension equals the order of the group.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: The primitive root of unity is the eigenvalue and gives distinct conjugates.
concepts.c:irreducible-polynomial: The minimal polynomial is $X^n - a$, which is irreducible.
concepts.c:galois-extension: A splitting field of a separable polynomial is Galois.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: A subgroup of the cyclic group $\mu_n$ is cyclic.

statement: Let $F$ be a [finite field](c:finite-field) with $q$ elements, $\theta$ a nontrivial [additive character](c:add-char) of $F$, and $\chi, \psi$ [multiplicative characters](c:mul-char) with value $0$ at $0$. Put $g(\chi) = \sum_x \chi(x)\theta(x)$ and $J(\chi, \psi) = \sum_x \chi(x)\psi(1 - x)$. If $\chi\psi$ is nontrivial, then $g(\chi)g(\psi) = g(\chi\psi)J(\chi, \psi)$.

hypotheses.text: The field $F$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field) with $q$ elements.
The map $\theta$ is a nontrivial [additive character](c:add-char) $F \to \mathbb{C}^\times$.
The maps $\chi$ and $\psi$ are [multiplicative characters](c:mul-char) of $F$ with value $0$ at $0$.

conclusion: If $\chi\psi$ is nontrivial, then $g(\chi)g(\psi) = g(\chi\psi)J(\chi, \psi)$; if also $\chi$ and $\psi$ are nontrivial, then $|J(\chi, \psi)|^2 = q$; and $J(\chi, \chi^{-1}) = -\chi(-1)$ for nontrivial $\chi$.

formal.difference: The declaration states part (i) only, as $g(\chi\varphi) J(\chi, \varphi) = g(\chi) g(\varphi)$ when $\chi\varphi$ is nontrivial. The absolute value and the case $J(\chi, \chi^{-1})$ are separate facts.

proofs.name: Expand the product of Gauss sums
proofs.slogan: Expand the product of Gauss sums, scale the variable, then read off the quotient and the special case.
proofs.scope: Parts (i), (ii) and (iii). Part (iii) needs no additive character.

roles.why: The finite field gives the substitution bijections $x = ty$ and $x \mapsto x/(1-x)$.
The additivity $\theta(x+y) = \theta(x)\theta(y)$ and the Gauss sum bound make the sums work.
Multiplicativity and orthogonality of $\chi\psi$ give the vanishing term and the factor $(\chi\psi)(t)$.

steps.slogan: Expand $g(\chi)g(\psi)$ and group the terms by $t = x + y$.
steps.detail: We have $g(\chi)g(\psi) = \sum_{x,y} \chi(x)\psi(y)\theta(x+y) = \sum_t \theta(t) S(t)$ with $S(t) = \sum_x \chi(x)\psi(t - x)$. For $t = 0$, $S(0) = \psi(-1)\sum_x (\chi\psi)(x) = 0$, because $\chi\psi$ is nontrivial.

steps.slogan: Substitute $x = ty$ to get $S(t) = (\chi\psi)(t)J(\chi, \psi)$ and prove part (i).
steps.detail: For $t \ne 0$, as $y$ runs over $F$, so does $x = ty$. Then $S(t) = \chi(t)\psi(t)\sum_y \chi(y)\psi(1 - y) = (\chi\psi)(t)J(\chi, \psi)$. Hence $g(\chi)g(\psi) = J(\chi, \psi)\sum_{t \ne 0} (\chi\psi)(t)\theta(t) = J(\chi, \psi)g(\chi\psi)$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $g(\chi\psi)$ and use the size of Gauss sums to get $|J|^2 = q$.
steps.detail: For nontrivial $\chi$, $\psi$ and $\chi\psi$, the Gauss sum theorem gives $|g|^2 = q$ for each. So $g(\chi\psi) \ne 0$ and $J = g(\chi)g(\psi)/g(\chi\psi)$. Then $|J|^2 = q \cdot q/q = q$.

steps.slogan: Reduce $J(\chi, \chi^{-1})$ to a sum of $\chi(x/(1-x))$ over $x \ne 0, 1$.
steps.detail: Let $\chi$ be nontrivial. The terms $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ vanish, because $\chi(0) = 0$ and $\chi^{-1}(0) = 0$. For other $x$ the term is $\chi(x)\chi^{-1}(1 - x) = \chi(x/(1 - x))$.

steps.slogan: Change the variable to $y = x/(1-x)$ and sum $\chi$ over $F \setminus \{0, -1\}$.
steps.detail: The map $x \mapsto x/(1-x)$ is a bijection from $F \setminus \{0, 1\}$ onto $F \setminus \{0, -1\}$ with inverse $y \mapsto y/(1+y)$. So $J(\chi, \chi^{-1}) = \sum_{y \ne 0, -1} \chi(y)$. Since $\sum_{y \ne 0} \chi(y) = 0$, removing $y = -1$ gives $-\chi(-1)$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three parts into the statement of the theorem.
steps.detail: Step 2 proves part (i). Step 3 proves part (ii). Step 5 proves part (iii).

concepts.c:finite-field: Bijections of the field allow the substitutions in the sums.
concepts.c:add-char: Additivity of $\theta$ groups the double sum by $t = x + y$.
concepts.c:mul-char: Multiplicativity and orthogonality of characters evaluate the inner sums.

statement: Let $N \ge 1$, $G = (\mathbb{Z}/N)^\times$ and $\hat G$ its group of characters. Extend each [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character) $\chi$ mod $N$ by $\chi(n) = 0$ when $\gcd(n, N) > 1$. Then $|\hat G| = \varphi(N)$, and for $a$ coprime to $N$ and every integer $b$, $\sum_\chi \bar\chi(a)\chi(b)$ is $\varphi(N)$ if $b \equiv a \pmod N$ and $0$ otherwise.

hypotheses.text: The number $N$ is a positive integer.
The group $G = (\mathbb{Z}/N)^\times$ is a [finite abelian group](c:finite-abelian-group).
The characters of $G$ take values in $\mathbb{C}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the orthogonality sum for a unit $a$ and any $b$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n$, with values in a ring that has enough roots of unity. It does not state the character count or the indicator formula.

proofs.name: Shift by a separating character
proofs.slogan: Count the characters, find one that separates a point from the identity, and shift the sum by it.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Integers not coprime to $N$ are treated apart, because every character vanishes on them.

roles.why: The modulus $N$ defines $G$ and $\varphi(N)$, and decides which integers are not coprime to $N$.
The group is finite and abelian, so it is a product of cyclic groups with a separating character.
Complex values have modulus $1$ on a finite group, so $\bar\chi = \chi^{-1}$ and roots of unity exist.

steps.slogan: Count the characters of $G$ with the structure theorem.
steps.detail: By the structure theorem, $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/n_1 \times \dots \times \mathbb{Z}/n_r$. A character is fixed by its values on the $r$ generators. Each value is an $n_k$-th [root of unity](c:root-of-unity) and any choice is allowed. So $|\hat G| = n_1 \cdots n_r = |G| = \varphi(N)$.

steps.slogan: Build a character $\chi_0$ with $\chi_0(g) \ne 1$ for each $g \ne 1$.
steps.detail:
Let $g = (g_1, \dots, g_r) 
e 0$ with $g_k 
e 0$. Define $\chi_0(h) = \exp(2\pi i\, h_k/n_k)$. This is a character, and $\chi_0(g) 
e 1$ because $0 < g_k < n_k$.

steps.slogan: Shift the sum over characters by $\chi_0$ to show that it is zero for $g \ne 1$.
steps.detail: Let $S = \sum_\chi \chi(g)$ with $g \ne 1$. The map $\chi \mapsto \chi_0\chi$ is a bijection of $\hat G$, so $S = \chi_0(g) S$. Since $\chi_0(g) \ne 1$, $S = 0$. For $g = 1$ the sum is $|\hat G| = \varphi(N)$.

steps.slogan: Prove the orthogonality relation for units and for integers not coprime to $N$.
steps.detail: For a unit $b$, $\bar\chi(a)\chi(b) = \chi(a^{-1}b)$ because $|\chi(a)| = 1$, and step 3 gives $\varphi(N)$ if $a^{-1}b = 1$ and $0$ otherwise. If $\gcd(b, N) > 1$, then $\chi(b) = 0$ for every $\chi$, and $b \not\equiv a$ because $a$ is a unit.

steps.slogan: Divide by $\varphi(N)$ to get the indicator formula of the residue class.
steps.detail: Divide the orthogonality relation by $\varphi(N)$. This gives $1_{n \equiv a \pmod N} = \frac{1}{\varphi(N)} \sum_\chi \bar\chi(a)\chi(n)$ for all $n$. The right side is a finite combination of the functions $n \mapsto \chi(n)$.

concepts.c:dirichlet-character: The filter is a combination of Dirichlet characters.
concepts.c:finite-abelian-group: The structure theorem describes the group and its characters.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: Character values on a generator are roots of unity.
